title: Menstrual Disorders in Adolescence: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges
article_subtype: Systematic literature review with narrative analysis
keywords: high risk for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
clinical_background: Adolescence spans ages 10 to 19 and includes pubertal changes. Menarche occurs at an average age of 12–13. During the first 2 years after menarche, immature hormonal regulation commonly produces anovulatory cycles and menstrual irregularity without an underlying disorder. Other menstrual abnormalities may be pathological and require timely recognition, treatment, or monitoring. Menstrual problems can affect adolescents’ well-being and quality of life.
objectives: Describe current diagnostic and therapeutic challenges involving physiological and pathological causes of menstrual irregularity in adolescence.
Distinguish adolescent menstrual disorders from those in adulthood and summarize their causes and treatment.
Evaluate the potential benefits of collaboration across clinical disciplines for adolescent care.
study_design: Review based on a systematic PubMed search conducted in April 2024 using “menstrual disorder adolescence”, supplemented by searches of relevant guidelines from the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) and the Arbeitsgemeinschaft der wissenschaftlichen medizinischen Fachgesellschaft (awmf). The authors screened 1724 abstracts, assessed 115 articles in full text, and analyzed the selected studies narratively using content analysis.

population.description: Adolescents between the ages of 10 and 19 with menstrual irregularities or disorders.
inclusion_criteria: English-language articles from the last 10 years.
Original articles providing relevant information about menstrual irregularities or disorders during adolescence.

primary: Menstrual irregularities and disorders arising from different causes.

interpretation: Menstrual irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche is often a physiological consequence of anovulation and an immature hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Other menstrual disorders have causes that warrant identification and appropriate care. The authors conclude that recognizing the distinction, avoiding a premature diagnosis, and coordinating care across specialties can improve adolescents’ quality of life and help prevent serious health problems.
clinical_implications: Anemia or dysmenorrhea accompanying menstrual irregularity requires treatment or further assessment, even when irregular cycles themselves may be physiological.
Heavy menstrual bleeding can impair participation in school, sport, and social life and can cause iron-deficiency anemia; an underlying coagulation disorder may complicate its management.

Prolonged estrogen deficiency can compromise bone health and affect cognitive and cardiovascular health. In premature ovarian insufficiency, the authors also describe reproductive and cardiovascular consequences.

In adolescents, menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenemia can indicate increased risk for PCOS without establishing that diagnosis. The associated metabolic, endometrial, and psychological risks make follow-up important.
Endometriosis may remain unrecognized when adolescent pain is inadequately investigated, while genital malformations that obstruct menstrual outflow can cause pain.
practice_implications: Assess the underlying cause of a menstrual disorder so that treatment and follow-up match the condition, while avoiding a diagnosis that prematurely stigmatizes or unsettles an adolescent.

Menstrual irregularity in the first 2 years after menarche generally does not require investigation unless disabling hypermenorrhea, anemia, or pain is present. Investigate a cycle that becomes irregular after it was regular.

Adapt examination to developmental stage and sexual activity. The usual assessment includes a medical history, physical examination, assessment of height and weight, and sonography of the internal genitalia; use additional investigations according to the clinical question.
Exclude pregnancy at the start of an amenorrhea assessment and, according to symptoms, consider excluding sexually transmitted diseases and trauma.

For heavy menstrual bleeding, assess hemoglobin and consider a coagulation disorder, particularly when personal or family bleeding history raises concern. Coordinate gynecological and hematological care when a coagulation disorder is present.

Treat juvenile hypermenorrhea with the aim of controlling bleeding, correcting anemia, establishing a regular cycle, and improving quality of life. The authors favor hormonal therapy, with the regimen chosen according to endometrial thickness, individual risks, and contraindications; iron replacement, transfusion, or tranexamic acid may also be needed. Avoid surgical curettage to protect the endometrium.

Explain that hormone replacement therapy does not provide contraception. An IUD containing levonorgestrel is another option for heavy menstrual bleeding in patients with or without a coagulation disorder.

For hypogonadotropic hypogonadism associated with inadequate energy intake or excessive activity, provide multidisciplinary care, support weight gain and adequate estrogenization, and consider reduced physical activity and increased calorie intake. Monitor bone density during treatment.
Evaluate possible causes of delayed puberty and consider puberty induction when indicated, including when delayed development remains likely because of chronic or mental illness.

For premature ovarian insufficiency, provide puberty induction when needed, continue appropriate hormone replacement and bone-health measures, monitor cardiovascular risks, and discuss fertility prospects and the possibility of pregnancy without contraception.

Assess the named androgen measurements and relevant differential diagnoses when investigating hyperandrogenemia. When findings raise concern for CAH, pursue the additional diagnostic steps described by the authors; address reproductive implications with affected patients and, when relevant, their partners.

Do not apply adult PCOS diagnostic criteria in adolescence or diagnose PCOS until 8 years after menarche. Classify adolescents with concerning findings as high risk, arrange individualized monitoring, and address menstrual, androgen-related, and metabolic problems through multidisciplinary care.

Consider endometriosis in adolescents with refractory or otherwise suggestive pain. The authors support conservative medication as first-line treatment and state that clinical findings can justify treatment without histological confirmation. Use GnRH analogs very cautiously because of bone effects; if symptoms persist, consider surgery at a center experienced in preserving ovarian reserve.

When a genital malformation is suspected, assess the external genitalia and use the imaging and hormonal investigations described by the authors. Consider surgical repair for malformations associated with recurrent pain.
Maintain contact across the transition between pediatric and gynecological care. Family doctors should work with relevant specialists so that adolescents do not lose access to support.
open_questions: The authors identify unresolved gaps in blood test reference ranges, drug dosages, and alternative treatment options for adolescents with menstrual disorders.
future_directions: The authors call for further research to address the identified gaps in blood test reference ranges, drug dosages, and alternative treatment options.

main_conclusion: Menstrual irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche is often physiological, but associated anemia or dysmenorrhea warrants treatment or investigation. Identifying pathological causes without prematurely labeling adolescents, and coordinating care across specialties, may improve quality of life and help prevent serious health problems.
narrative_summary: This review examined the causes, diagnosis, and treatment of menstrual disorders in adolescence. The authors searched PubMed in April 2024, screened 1724 abstracts, assessed 115 full texts, and included 71 articles in a narrative analysis; they also consulted relevant ESHRE and awmf guidance. In the first 2 years after menarche, irregular cycles commonly reflect anovulation and immaturity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis rather than disease. Disabling heavy bleeding, anemia, or pain are exceptions that require attention. The review distinguishes this physiological pattern from conditions including bleeding disorders, amenorrhea, hypogonadism, premature ovarian insufficiency, hyperandrogenemia, endometriosis, and genital malformations. Assessment is guided by symptoms and developmental stage and may include history, examination, abdominal sonography, and selected laboratory or other investigations. Treatment depends on the cause: options discussed include hormonal management of heavy bleeding, correction of anemia, restoration of adequate estrogenization in hypogonadism, and appropriate management of suspected endometriosis or obstructive malformations. The authors caution against diagnosing PCOS prematurely in adolescence and favor individualized monitoring when features indicate increased risk. They emphasize collaboration among primary care, pediatric, gynecological, and hematological clinicians, particularly when adolescents fall between pediatric and adult services. Remaining knowledge gaps include blood-test reference ranges, drug doses, and alternative treatments.

main_findings.description: Menstrual irregularity shortly after menarche is often physiological because ovulatory function has not yet matured.
main_findings.context: At 2 years after menarche; the review cites prior literature for this estimate.

main_findings.description: Disabling heavy bleeding, anemia, or pain are exceptions to the review's advice against investigating otherwise uncomplicated early menstrual irregularity.
main_findings.context: Applies during the first 2 years after menarche.

main_findings.description: The review defines hypermenorrhea by both prolonged bleeding and high blood loss.
main_findings.value: longer than 7 days; more than 80 mL
main_findings.context: The thresholds are drawn from cited literature.

main_findings.description: A coagulation disorder accounts for a reported proportion of hypermenorrhea cases.
main_findings.context: A cited estimate; the review identifies von Willebrand syndrome, platelet dysfunction, and factor 7 or 8 deficiency among the differential diagnoses.

main_findings.description: The review presents hormonal treatment as the preferred approach to juvenile hypermenorrhea and differentiates treatment according to endometrial thickness.
main_findings.metric: treatment duration and dose for a thickened endometrium
main_findings.value: 14 days; dydrogesterone 2 × 10 mg daily or medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily
main_findings.context: Progestogen monotherapy follows sonographic assessment. For a thin endometrium, the review describes estrogenization before endometrial transformation.

main_findings.description: For acute heavy bleeding that does not stop with the usual dose, the review describes a temporary higher-dose oral contraceptive regimen.
main_findings.context: Administration continues until bleeding decreases, followed by reduction to two and then one tablet daily; individual contraindications and risks must be considered.

main_findings.description: Hospital admission may occasionally be needed for juvenile hypermenorrhea, particularly with marked anemia.
main_findings.context: The review characterizes hospitalization as necessary only in rare cases.

main_findings.description: The review reports that tranexamic acid appears comparably effective to hormonal treatment for hypermenorrhea.
main_findings.context: This qualified comparison is drawn from cited literature; no numerical comparative estimate is supplied.

main_findings.description: An IUD containing levonorgestrel is described as effective for heavy bleeding both with and without coagulation disorders.
main_findings.context: The cited literature does not indicate an increased IUD expulsion rate in patients with coagulation disorders.

main_findings.description: The review distinguishes primary from secondary amenorrhea using age at menarche and time without menstruation.
main_findings.value: until the age of 16; more than 90 days
main_findings.context: Primary amenorrhea is absence of menarche by the stated age; secondary amenorrhea concerns someone who has previously menstruated.

main_findings.description: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is identified as the most common cause of primary and secondary amenorrhea; in adolescents, competitive sport, stress, and eating disorders are usual causes.
main_findings.context: The review attributes these observations to cited literature.

main_findings.description: Menstruation generally resumes after restoration of normal weight, although amenorrhea persists despite weight gain in a subset.
main_findings.metric: time to menstrual return; proportion with persistent amenorrhea
main_findings.context: Reported for weight-related hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; the proportion refers to cases with persistent amenorrhea after weight gain.

main_findings.description: The review warns that bone density after hypothalamic amenorrhea can take years to recover or may never reach the expected peak, with continuing fracture risk.
main_findings.context: Discussed in connection with low estrogenization and osteoporosis.

main_findings.description: Delayed puberty is described by absent breast development or a prolonged interruption in pubertal progression.
main_findings.metric: age threshold, interruption duration, and frequency
main_findings.context: The frequency refers to delayed puberty among adolescents.

main_findings.description: The review advises evaluating possible causes and considering pubertal induction if breast development has not begun by the specified age and menarche has not occurred by the specified age.
main_findings.context: Age of 13 applies to breast development; age of 16 applies to menarche.

main_findings.description: Premature ovarian insufficiency is uncommon in adolescence despite a higher prevalence stated for premature ovarian failure overall.
main_findings.context: The first estimate concerns ovarian failure before the age of 40; the second concerns people under 20.

main_findings.description: Evidence supporting premature ovarian insufficiency combines a raised FSH measurement with sustained oligo- or amenorrhea.
main_findings.metric: FSH threshold and duration of cycle disorder
main_findings.context: If diagnosis remains uncertain, the review recommends repeating FSH assessment after 4–6 weeks.

main_findings.description: For adolescents requiring induction of puberty, the review describes gradually increasing low-dose 17-βoestradiol and subsequent progesterone for endometrial protection.
main_findings.metric: starting age, escalation period, and progesterone timing
main_findings.context: Progesterone may instead begin when breakthrough bleeding occurs; the estradiol approach is attributed to the ESHRE guidelines.

main_findings.description: Breast development during the described puberty-induction treatment usually begins before it is complete.
main_findings.context: These timings are presented in the discussion of estrogen replacement for premature ovarian insufficiency.

main_findings.description: The review gives an estradiol target corresponding to regularly menstruating women and advises continuing hormone replacement until the stated average menopausal age.
main_findings.context: Applies to maintenance treatment after completion of pubertal development in premature ovarian insufficiency.

main_findings.description: Spontaneous pregnancy remains possible with premature ovarian failure, although the review describes egg donation as the only option offering a real chance of pregnancy.
main_findings.context: The possibility of pregnancy is relevant when discussing contraception with adolescents.

main_findings.description: The review cautions that AMH in adolescence must be interpreted against an age-dependent range rather than its later peak.
main_findings.metric: childhood and adolescent AMH range; age at peak
main_findings.context: The age refers to when the review says AMH reaches its peak.

main_findings.description: The review attributes most cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia to mutation of the 21-hydroxylase gene and reports a lower frequency of deficiency among women with hyperandrogenemia.
main_findings.metric: proportion of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases; proportion of women with hyperandrogenemia
main_findings.context: The latter proportion concerns women with a 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

main_findings.description: Elevated early-cycle 17-OH progesterone warrants assessment for CAH; the review also specifies a rise after ACTH testing that prompts genetic testing.
main_findings.context: The first is the early-cycle concentration; the second is the increase after ACTH administration.

main_findings.description: The review states that adult Rotterdam criteria should not be applied to adolescents and cautions against diagnosing PCOS too early after menarche.
main_findings.context: Adolescents with oligomenorrhoea and hyperandrogenemia are instead described as at high risk for later PCOS.

main_findings.description: Polycystic ovarian appearance alone is unsuitable for diagnosing PCOS in adolescents because it is also seen in girls of this age group.
main_findings.context: The proportion is drawn from cited literature and does not represent a PCOS diagnosis rate.

main_findings.description: The review describes androgen reduction with anti-androgenic treatment as improving acne and hirsutism, while visible improvement in hair growth can be delayed.
main_findings.metric: time until an effect on hair growth may become apparent
main_findings.context: Discussed for treatment of adolescents at high risk for PCOS.

main_findings.description: Metformin is described as a possible aid to weight reduction, particularly with insulin resistance and higher BMI, but the review states that this treatment works only alongside exercise.
main_findings.metric: BMI threshold and maximum daily dose
main_findings.context: Gradual dose escalation is described to limit gastrointestinal effects.

main_findings.description: Endometriosis is reported in a small proportion of adolescent women and may be suspected when characteristic pain persists or is refractory.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature; the review also notes dysmenorrhea, acyclic lower abdominal pain, dysuria, dyschezia, and dyspareunia as suggestive symptoms.

main_findings.description: The review notes that endometriosis diagnosis can be delayed and that treatment may be justified by clinical findings without histological confirmation.
main_findings.context: It identifies a low ultrasound detection rate and reluctance to undertake surgery in adolescents as possible contributors to delayed diagnosis.

main_findings.description: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome is presented as a genital malformation often recognized after primary amenorrhea.
main_findings.context: The review describes uterine aplasia and associated renal and skeletal malformations.

main_findings.description: The review concludes that adolescent menstrual disorders have varied causes and that determining the underlying cause supports appropriate treatment without prematurely stigmatizing patients.
main_findings.context: It emphasizes interdisciplinary care and identifies unresolved questions about blood-test reference ranges, drug doses, and alternative treatments.

notable_adverse_events: Metformin: gastrointestinal effects, including diarrhea, are described without a reported rate.
GnRH analogs: adverse effects on bone and a long-term osteoporosis risk are described without a reported rate.
Estrogen used for pubertal induction: accelerated bone maturation and a possible halt to longitudinal growth are discussed without a reported rate.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Adolescence spans ages 10 to 19 and is shaped by puberty. Menarche occurs, on average, at age 12–13. Anovulatory cycles and irregular bleeding are common after menarche, particularly during the first 2 years. This review examines diagnostic and treatment challenges posed by physiological and pathological menstrual irregularities and considers the value of interdisciplinary care. A PubMed search conducted in April 2024 used “menstrual disorder adolescence”; 1724 abstracts were screened, and relevant publications from the last 10 years were considered. Searches of European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) and Arbeitsgemeinschaft der wissenschaftlichen medizinischen Fachgesellschaft (awmf) guidelines supplemented the search. Although immaturity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis can cause physiological irregularity, other abnormalities are pathological and require recognition and treatment. Greater awareness across specialties and cooperation between them may improve affected adolescents’ quality of life.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Adolescence covers ages 10 to 19 and involves substantial physical, psychological, emotional, moral, and intellectual development during puberty. Menstrual health matters to adolescents’ well-being and quality of life; after menarche, girls may feel uncertain about menstruation and need assistance when problems arise. The review addresses the causes, diagnosis, and treatment of physiological and pathological menstrual irregularities and the potential benefit of interdisciplinary care. Anovulatory cycles caused by an immature gonadal axis commonly produce physiological irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche. Other abnormalities are pathological and warrant timely recognition, treatment, and monitoring.

document_sections.heading: 2. Review Literature Search
document_sections.content: The review seeks to distinguish adolescent menstrual disorders from those in adults and describe their causes and treatment. A systematic PubMed search in April 2024 used “menstrual disorder adolescence”. Eligible relevant articles were published within the last 10 years and were in English. Investigators screened 1724 abstracts, selected 115 articles for full-text assessment, analyzed them narratively using content analysis, and included 71 in the review. The principal variables were menstrual irregularities and disorders with differing causes. Inclusion concerned good-quality studies involving adolescent patients, including original articles with relevant information. A supplementary search examined pertinent literature in European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) and Arbeitsgemeinschaft der wissenschaftlichen medizinischen Fachgesellschaft (awmf) guidelines. Figure 1 presents the PRISMA selection flow.

document_sections.heading: 3. The Onset of Puberty as a Transition from Childhood to Adolescence
document_sections.content: Puberty starts as hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neuronal activity changes. GnRH release initially occurs at night and later becomes pulsatile during the day as well. GnRH stimulates pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) release. LH and FSH regulate gonadal testosterone, estradiol, and progesterone secretion, leading to secondary sexual development. Figure 2 depicts hormonal regulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovary axis and identifies GABA as gamma–aminobutyric acid.

document_sections.heading: 4. Menarche and the Menstrual Cycle in Adolescence
document_sections.content: Physical pubertal development lasts around 3 years. It begins with thelarche at an average age of 11 years, and menarche follows breast development by an average of 2 years, marking the end of the growth spurt. Early cycles are frequently anovulatory; 2 years after menarche, up to 85% remain anovulatory. Follicular persistence and irregular cycles can therefore be physiological consequences of gonadal-axis immaturity. Ovulation becomes regular toward the end of puberty. Menstrual irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche does not require investigation unless disabling hypermenorrhea, anemia, or pain occurs.

document_sections.heading: 5. Special Features in Diagnostics
document_sections.content: Usual assessment comprises a detailed history, physical examination, sonography of internal genitalia, and measurement of height and weight. Examination should reflect the adolescent’s developmental stage and sexual activity. Tanner stages categorize pubertal development and help assess age-appropriate hormonal-axis function and progression. External genital inspection uses gentle separation and lateral or caudal traction of the labia majora; a pediatric speculum is seldom needed. Abdominal sonography is performed with a full bladder. It assesses the uterus and ovaries, including uterine shape as an indicator of estrogenization, endometrial thickness, antral follicles, cysts, and follicular persistence. Genetic assessment, magnetic tomography (MRI), or, rarely, laparoscopy may address specific diagnostic questions. A GnRH test can assess pituitary function; an ACTH test can be useful when congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is suspected. In amenorrhea, a progestogen test can assess endogenous estrogen activity and endometrial function; in uterine amenorrhea, an estrogen–progestogen test can assess endometrial responsiveness. Hormone measurements, bone-age or bone-density assessment, glucose-metabolism assessment, and testing for suspected chronic disease are reserved for particular questions. Pregnancy, sexually transmitted diseases, and trauma should be excluded according to symptoms. Figures 3 and 4 illustrate abdominal sonographic views of an adolescent ovary and uterus.

document_sections.heading: 6. Menstrual Irregularities and Disorders in Adolescence 6.1. Dysfunctional, Juvenile Hypermenorrhea
document_sections.content: Hypermenorrhea means bleeding lasting longer than 7 days with blood loss of more than 80 mL. It is a common adolescent gynecological complaint. Heavy blood loss can restrict school, sport, and social participation, reduce quality of life, and accompany increased depression; iron-deficiency anemia can cause serious health problems. During the first few years after menarche, anovulation associated with hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian immaturity often causes follicular persistence and increased uterine bleeding, a feature of normal pubertal development rather than necessarily a clinical problem. Persistent juvenile bleeding is attributed to insufficient GnRH and LH release and disrupted regulatory feedback, with irregular estrogen changes, a prolonged estrogen phase, or disturbed estrogen–progestogen balance. Differential diagnosis must include a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand syndrome, platelet dysfunction, or factor 7 or 8 deficiency. Personal or family bleeding history strengthens suspicion. A coagulation disorder causes hypermenorrhea in 7–62% of cases; when present, managing bleeding can be difficult and calls for joint gynecological and hematological care to prevent recurrent bleeding that lowers hemoglobin (Hb). Hb should be measured because adolescents may struggle to judge blood loss; anemia-related tiredness, fatigue, and dizziness diminish quality of life. Affected girls often do not seek medical care or receive adequate diagnosis and treatment. Hormonal treatment is the preferred approach. Following sonographic assessment, an excessively thick endometrium can be treated with progestogen alone for 14 days, such as dydrogesterone 2 × 10 mg daily or medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily. With a thin endometrium, estrogenization followed by transformation is needed: options include estrogen alone for 10 days followed by an estrogen–progestogen combination, an oral contraceptive—which is most commonly used, particularly for prophylaxis—or norethisterone acetate 2.5–5 mg daily for 10 days. The latter has a partial estrogenic effect but is not freely available in every country. For acute bleeding that does not stop with usual dosing, a contraceptive pill containing at least 30 µg of ethinylestradiol can be given every 6–8 h until bleeding decreases, then reduced to two and subsequently one tablet daily. Individual contraindications and risks must be considered. Depending on risk, a progesterone-only pill can be used; acute heavy bleeding may require a higher progestogen dose, such as double the dose of desogestrel. Hospital admission is occasionally necessary, particularly when Hb is below 8 g/dL. Oral contraception and hormone replacement therapy can provide prophylaxis and can continue during overt anemia until Hb recovers, but hormone replacement therapy does not provide contraception. A levonorgestrel-containing IUD (intrauterine device) is another effective option with or without a coagulation disorder, without an increased expulsion rate reported in those with coagulation disorders. Insertion can be harder in adolescents, especially before sexual intercourse, and may require sedation. Heavy bleeding may also require iron replacement, transfusion, or tranexamic acid. Tranexamic acid is particularly relevant when hormones are declined or contraindicated and appears as effective as hormonal treatment for hypermenorrhea. Surgical curettage should be avoided to preserve the endometrium. Figure 5 illustrates marked endometrial thickening in a 12-year-old girl with juvenile hypermenorrhea. Treatment aims to stop bleeding, correct anemia, establish a regular cycle, and improve quality of life.

document_sections.heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
document_sections.content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

document_sections.heading: 6.3. Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is described as the most common cause of both primary and secondary amenorrhea and involves impaired hypothalamic function and gonadotropin release. In adolescents it is usually associated with competitive sport, stress, or an eating disorder. Sports activity and body-fat mass correlate with amenorrhea likelihood and adverse bone-density effects. The “female athlete triad”, also termed “relative energy deficiency in sport” by the International Olympic Committee, combines low energy availability, menstrual disturbance, and low bone density. Calorie restriction can disrupt menstruation even when BMI is within the normal range; eating disorders should therefore be treated early to prevent lasting harm. Less frequent causes include brain tumors, craniocerebral trauma, perinatal asphyxia, brain radiotherapy, systemic disease such as histiocytosis, Wilson’s disease, or thalassemia, and genetic defects such as Kallmann syndrome, septo-optic dysplasia, or a GnRH receptor defect. Testing shows low-to-normal gonadotropins and usually low estradiol; sonography may show a thin endometrium and ovaries without follicular maturation. Even brief dietary restriction can produce a prepubertal gonadotropin-secretion pattern, particularly for LH. LH pulses then become too infrequent for follicular maturation, resulting in estrogen deficiency and menstrual disorders, including amenorrhea. Adequate estrogenization supports peak bone mass and long-term skeletal health. Menstruation usually resumes approximately 6–12 months after normal weight is restored, but amenorrhea persists despite weight gain in around 10–30% of cases. Bone density can require years to recover or may never reach an appropriate peak, leaving lifelong excess fracture risk associated with osteoporosis. Care should involve psychologists and psychiatrists, with bone-density measurements during treatment. The preferred approach is weight gain, restoration of normal cycles, and adequate estrogenization, potentially requiring less exercise and increased calories and BMI into the normal range. Estrogenization also influences neurological and psychological development and health. Gynecological treatment emphasizes estrogenization to limit long-term effects, particularly on bone. Estradiol appears most beneficial for this purpose, although achieving estrogenization is especially important; contraceptive pills and a contraceptive patch, particularly for patients with bulimia, are alternatives with positive effects. Progesterone is also needed for endometrial transformation and protection. Vitamin D and calcium should be supplemented; calcium supplementation is unnecessary with a normal diet, but 1000–1500 mg daily should be supplied in an eating disorder such as anorexia nervosa.

document_sections.heading: 6.4. Delayed Puberty/Pubertas Tarda
document_sections.content: Delayed puberty, formerly “pubertas tarda”, means absent breast development after around 13.5 years or interruption of pubertal progression for more than 18 months. It occurs in 0.3% of adolescents and is frequently a nonpathological normal variant. Constitutional delay in growth and development often clusters in families. Nevertheless, causes should be evaluated and puberty induction considered when breast development has not begun by age 13 and menarche has not occurred by age 16. Family pubertal history may support constitutional familial delay. A pathological cause becomes more likely with older age at initial assessment. Evaluation should consider competitive sport, malnutrition, drugs such as cannabis, chronic diseases including anorexia, chronic inflammatory bowel disease, and cystic fibrosis, and malformations; gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, and genetic disorders should be excluded. Recommended assessment includes clinical examination, bone age, exclusion of chronic disease, and blood testing of thyroid function, LH, FSH, estradiol, and prolactin. Low LH and FSH in constitutional delay or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism resemble a prepubertal hormone profile, whereas LH and FSH are significantly elevated in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Depending on the suspected cause, olfactory testing, a GnRH test, brain MRI, abdominal ultrasound, or genetic testing may help. Prader Willi and Leopard syndrome are other possible contexts. Despite differing causes, puberty induction is usually needed to establish a normal phenotype and sufficient estrogen. It is also recommended when delayed development remains possible because of chronic or mental illness, to reduce long-term consequences or improve well-being. Induction generally starts at 11–13 years. Estradiol is increased at 6-month intervals under close monitoring; after approximately 2 years, progestogens may initiate bleeding, for example Utrogestan 200 mg cyclically for 14 days. Table 1 outlines age-specific puberty induction and estrogen replacement, including dose escalation and later cyclic progesterone.

document_sections.heading: 6.5. Premature Ovarian Insufficiency
document_sections.content: Premature ovarian failure is loss of ovarian function before age 40 and has a prevalence of approximately 1%. Genetic causes include Turner syndrome, a Fragile X (FRAXA) premutation, XY gonadal dysgenesis, and androgen resistance. Associations with Addison’s disease or Hashimoto’s thyroiditis may indicate autoimmune destruction of follicles. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ovarian surgery for malignancy can cause iatrogenic loss of ovarian tissue. In adolescence, premature ovarian insufficiency is rare, affecting around 1:10,000 people under age 20. Evidence for diagnosis consists of FSH above 25 IU/L together with oligo- or amenorrhea for at least 4 months. FSH need not be measured on a particular cycle day; if diagnosis is uncertain, repeat assessment after 4–6 weeks. Further recommended tests include karyotype, FRAXA premutation, 21-hydroxylase, and anti-Thyroid antibodies. Many cases have no identifiable cause and are termed idiopathic POI; adolescents frequently do not receive a precise diagnosis. Depending on onset, induction may be needed for secondary sexual development. ESHRE guidance describes starting low-dose 17-βoestradiol at 11–13 years and increasing it over 2–3 years. Tanner stages, growth, and internal-genital sonography should be checked every 3–6 months. Because estrogen accelerates skeletal maturation and might curtail height gain, the starting age is debated; low-dose treatment can begin at 12–13 years without height loss. Turner syndrome, particularly Mosaic Turner syndrome, may remain unrecognized until adolescence. In Turner syndrome, growth hormone is administered in childhood at age 4–6 years to improve eventual height; affected girls lack the growth spurt normally triggered by endogenous estrogen. Treatment seeks acceptable final height, increased bone mass, and normal psychosexual development without psychosocial stigmatization. An assessment of girls with Turner syndrome found that low estrogenization accompanying primary amenorrhea was associated with reduced bone density and consequent greater fracture risk. If diagnosis is late, estradiol may be increased more rapidly. Transdermal delivery is preferred because it produces more physiological estrogen levels with less thrombosis risk. Breast development usually starts after 6 months and is complete after 2 years. On breakthrough bleeding or after 2 years, regular progesterone should begin to protect the endometrium and prevent hyperplasia. Table 1 summarizes induction and replacement schedules. After puberty, recommended maintenance options with progesterone are a transdermal estradiol patch delivering 100–200 µg, 2 mg of estradiol gel, 2–4 mg of oral estradiol, or an appropriately dosed combined contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy. The target is an estradiol concentration comparable to that of a regularly menstruating woman, averaging 180–370 pmol/L. Hormone replacement should continue to the average menopausal age of 51 years. Untreated premature ovarian failure is associated with shorter life expectancy, chiefly because of cardiovascular disease; a balanced diet, exercise, smoking cessation, and cardiovascular-risk monitoring are recommended. Depression is more frequent, and estrogen deficiency increases vulnerability to it. Local estrogenization can treat symptoms or sexual dysfunction related to vulvovaginal atrophy. For bone health, exercise and adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D, or supplementation when dietary intake is insufficient, are central alongside hormone replacement. No intervention increases ovarian activity. Patients should receive information about future fertility: spontaneous pregnancy occurs at around 5%, while egg donation offers the only realistic chance of pregnancy. Even a small possibility of pregnancy warrants attention to contraception to avoid unintended teenage pregnancy. Childhood and adolescent anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) values normally range from 0.7–7.5 ng/mL and peak at age 25; a low adolescent value must be interpreted in light of this not-yet-peaked physiological range to avoid unnecessary concern.

document_sections.heading: 6.6. Hyperandrogenemia
document_sections.content: Hyperandrogenemia and its underlying causes form another group of menstrual disorders. Adolescent manifestations include acne, hirsutism, alopecia, oligo-/amenorrhea, pubertas praecox, and clitoral hypertrophy. Rapid virilization suggests a rare androgen-producing tumor. In obesity, adipose tissue adds to androgen production at physiological sources including the adrenal cortex, ovary, and periphery. Initial diagnostic hormone assessment covers testosterone, androstenedione, DHEAS, and 17-Hydroxy-(OH)-progesterone (17-OHP), alongside exclusion of prolactinoma and hypothyroidism, which may accompany hyperandrogenemia. Only free androgens are active.

document_sections.heading: 6.7. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)/Late-Onset Adrenogential Syndrome (AGS)
document_sections.content: This autosomal recessive condition is attributed to mutation of the 21-hydroxylase gene on chromosome 6 in approximately 90% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases, reducing enzyme activity by 30–50%. Most affected people have compound heterozygous or homozygous mutations; a single affected gene does not produce the disease. Approximately 4% of women with hyperandrogenemia have 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Early-cycle 17-OH progesterone above 2 ng/mL calls for exclusion of CAH as a major differential diagnosis of PCOS. Insufficient or absent 21-hydroxylase raises its substrate 17-OH-progesterone, reduces cortisol, increases ACTH, and thereby stimulates adrenal steroid synthesis, including androgen production. A 17-OH progesterone result >2 ng/mL warrants additional assessment. A dexamethasone inhibition test can help exclude Cushing’s syndrome: cortisol suppression is checked the morning after 1 mg of dexamethasone at 11 pm. In an ACTH test, ACTH is given intravenously; a rise in 17-OH progesterone of more than 2.5 ng/mL should prompt genetic testing for 21hydroxylase deficiency. Less common causes of CAH include 11-β-hydroxylase deficiency and a 3-β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase defect. Girls may have no symptoms for a long period. Manifestations range from early pubarche, tall stature, and accelerated bone maturation to clitoral hypertrophy, hirsutism, acne, alopecia, oligo-amenorrhea, and infertility. Future childbearing requires attention because a partner who also carries a mutation creates a risk of a child homozygous for a severe mutation, with very low enzyme activity, severe salt-wasting CAH, and possible genital virilization in girls. The authors advise diagnosing both partners, discussing the risk, and, if necessary, giving cortisol during pregnancy, since later full correction may be difficult or impossible depending on severity. Outside that context, glucocorticoids are recommended only for puberty praecox or accelerated bone age. An anti-androgen pill can regulate cycles and reduce androgens, addressing both hyperandrogenic symptoms and menstrual disturbance. Follicular stimulation can help when pregnancy is desired because ovulation is often insufficient.

document_sections.heading: 6.8. High Risk for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
document_sections.content: An adolescent symptom constellation can indicate high risk for future PCOS. In adults, Rotterdam criteria confirm PCOS when two of three features are present: oligo-/amenorrhea, hyperandrogenemia or signs of androgenization, and sonomorphological evidence of polycystic ovaries. These criteria should not be applied in adolescence, and PCOS should not be diagnosed until 8 years after menarche. Blood androgen concentrations reach adult female levels only at ages 12–15, and clear cut-offs are lacking. Androgens originate in the adrenal cortex, periphery, and adipose tissue. Polycystic ovarian appearance is unsuitable as an adolescent diagnostic criterion because around 33% of girls of this age have it on sonography; its presence alone does not establish PCOS. Oligomenorrhoea together with hyperandrogenemia appears to signal increased later PCOS risk. Adolescents should therefore be classified as high risk and followed closely without premature diagnostic labeling or distress. Individualized monitoring is important because associated risks include metabolic syndrome, impaired glucose tolerance, type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, sterility, endometrial cancer, and depression. The Ferriman–Gallwey score permits patient assessment of body hair in hirsutism; Figure 6 illustrates pronounced hirsutism and obesity permagna in a 16-year-old girl at high risk for PCOS. Possible laboratory findings include LH/FSH quotient >>2, Homa index >2.5, abnormal oral glucose tolerance or HbA1c, elevated AMH, and, with obesity, low SHBG or dyslipidemia. Normal 17-OH progesterone helps distinguish this constellation from congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). None of these additional laboratory abnormalities is a diagnostic criterion. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other hyperandrogenemia causes. Etiology remains largely uncertain, although genetic and environmental contributions appear possible. Several mechanisms may lead to anovulation; the proposed “two-hit” theory combines predisposition with a trigger such as insulin resistance. PCOS treatment should be multidisciplinary. An anti-androgen contraceptive pill is the primary treatment for cycle disturbance; oral contraception is also preferred for acne, hirsutism, and regular endometrial transformation during amenorrhea. Cyproterone acetate, dienogest, chlormadinone acetate, and drospirenone are described as potent antiandrogenic progestins. Lowering androgens improves acne and hirsutism, although visible improvement in hair growth can take a good 6–9 months. With obesity, exercise and nutritional counseling are important aspects of lifestyle change; collaboration with dieticians or an obesity center can help, and multidisciplinary care improves treatment success. Metformin is an insulin sensitizer that can support weight reduction, particularly with insulin resistance and BMI over 25 kg/m2. Its dose is increased gradually to a maximum of 2000 mg daily to limit gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea, and it works only in combination with exercise. Dermatological support may help acne; laser treatment can be tried for distressing hirsutism, and eflornithine cream can slow facial hair growth and reduce shaving frequency. Marked obesity, thrombophilia-related coagulation disorder, arterial hypertension, or nicotine use may contraindicate oral contraception; progestogen-only preparations such as cyproterone acetate or drospirenone can then be tried. Individual contraceptive needs must be considered. Without endometrial transformation during amenorrhea, hyperplasia may arise. Given metabolic risk, close OGTT monitoring, weight and blood-pressure checks even in slim girls, and lipid assessment are sensible to enable timely referral for treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6.9. Dysmenorrhea with Endometriosis and Genital Malformations
document_sections.content: Endometriosis and genital malformations, which usually produce dysmenorrhea, are addressed briefly for completeness.

document_sections.heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
document_sections.content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6.11. Genital Malformations
document_sections.content: Primary amenorrhea is the main manifestation of genital malformations. Painful examples chiefly include hymenal atresia, uterus didelphys with a vaginal septum obstructing one horn, and a rudimentary uterine horn whose endometrium bleeds periodically. Any malformation blocking menstrual outflow can cause dysmenorrhea; difficulty using a tampon can provide another clue. Hymenal atresia is generally isolated rather than associated with more extensive malformations. Examination shows vaginal closure and may identify hematocolpos or hematometra. Management depends on the specific anomaly; malformations causing recurrent pain should be repaired surgically. Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome has an incidence of 1:5000, may escape recognition in childhood, and presents with primary amenorrhea. Impaired development of the Müller ducts produces uterine aplasia and is associated with renal and skeletal anomalies. Neovaginal reconstruction can enable largely normal sexual function. Assessment should include external genital inspection, abdominal ultrasound with a full bladder, renal ultrasound, and hormone testing to exclude hormonal causes. MRI is the first-line diagnostic procedure for a suspected adolescent malformation; diagnostic laparoscopy may follow if needed. Once the anomaly is defined, the need for surgery can be determined and treatment initiated.

document_sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Adolescent menstrual disorders have multiple causes. Unlike in adulthood, irregularity during the 2 years after menarche often reflects anovulation and hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian immaturity without pathological significance; resulting anemia or dysmenorrhea always requires treatment or investigation. Identifying the underlying cause enables appropriate treatment and follow-up, while avoiding premature diagnoses that could stigmatize or unsettle adolescents. A care gap can arise when girls are too old for pediatric care but do not feel ready to attend gynecology services. Family doctors should maintain contact and coordinate with other disciplines. Pediatricians, gynecologists, family doctors, and hematologists can work together to support quality of life and prevent serious health problems. The review summarizes current diagnostic and treatment knowledge but identifies gaps concerning blood-test reference ranges, medication doses, and alternative treatments. Further research is needed to address those gaps.
